metadata.title: Associations between time spent communicating with parents, teacher self-efficacy, and stress: The role of professional development
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher microdata with a two-stage sampling design: schools are selected with probability proportional to size, and then about 20 teachers per selected school are randomly sampled (all teachers if fewer than 20). For individual-country analyses, the authors use the respective teacher sample weights; for the pooled cross-national analysis, they rescale the teacher sample weights to create senate weights so that each country contributes equally. The regression models are adjusted for these teacher weights and use school fixed effects with standard errors clustered at the school level. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported, so uncertainty quantification relies on clustered standard errors rather than replicate-based variance estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample drawn from TALIS 2018 teacher survey across 45 countries (excluding Australia and the Netherlands due to low response rates; excluding France, Russia, and Spain due to missing key variables). Included teachers who worked full-time and taught at least one academic subject; restricted to schools with at least 2 teachers (excluding 441 school samples with fewer than 2 teachers). Removed outliers with total working hours per week >80 or <20 (top 1% of the pooled distribution and bottom tail). Applied listwise deletion for missingness on all variables used (missing rates 0.1%–2%). Final pooled sample: 122,584 teachers in 12,034 primary and secondary schools across 45 countries (23,484 primary and 99,100 secondary teachers).

main_findings.performance_metrics: School fixed-effects regression with teacher sample weights and clustered SEs. Key coefficient: Time spent communicating with parents (hour) = 0.031 SD increase in self-efficacy (p < .001). Model includes controls; Observations = 122,584; Number of school-by-country = 12,034.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data pooled across 45 countries, the study leveraged time spent communicating with parents (hours) and stress-related covariates (including parental stress and other stressors) to predict standardized teacher self-efficacy, finding that each additional hour of parent communication was associated with a 0.031 SD increase in self-efficacy (p < .001) after school fixed effects and controls. This indicates that encouraging structured teacher–parent communication may strengthen teachers’ professional confidence, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.performance_metrics: School fixed-effects regression with teacher sample weights and clustered SEs. Key coefficient: Time spent communicating with parents (hour) = 0.062 SD increase in parent-related stress (p < .001). Model includes controls; Observations = 122,584; Number of school-by-country = 12,034.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data pooled across 45 countries, the study leveraged time spent communicating with parents (hours) and self-efficacy-related covariates to predict standardized parent-related stress, finding that each additional hour of parent communication was associated with a 0.062 SD increase in parent-related stress (p < .001) after school fixed effects and controls. This indicates that policies promoting parent communication should also include stress-mitigation supports (e.g., training and boundaries), because the same communication time that boosts self-efficacy is more strongly linked to higher stress.

main_findings.target_variable: Moderating effect of professional development (PD) on communication–self-efficacy and communication–stress associations
top_predictors: PD for working with parents × Time spent communicating with parents (hours)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Interaction model with school fixed effects and clustered SEs. PD main effects: PD for working with parents = +0.153 SD self-efficacy (p < .001) and +0.100 SD parent-related stress (p < .001) in Table 3. Interaction terms: PD × Time = -0.008 (not significant) for self-efficacy; PD × Time = -0.040 SD (p < .001) for parent-related stress. Observations = 122,584.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher survey data pooled across 45 countries, the study leveraged PD participation and its interaction with parent-communication time to predict teacher self-efficacy and parent-related stress, finding that PD did not significantly moderate the communication–self-efficacy association but significantly reduced the communication–stress association (interaction = -0.040 SD, p < .001). This indicates that professional development focused on teacher–parent collaboration can protect teachers from the stress-inducing aspects of frequent parent communication, even if it does not further amplify the self-efficacy benefits.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher survey data pooled across 45 countries to examine how time spent communicating with parents relates to teacher self-efficacy and parent-related stress, and whether professional development (PD) moderates these associations. Using school fixed-effects regression with teacher sample weights and school-clustered standard errors, the authors find that each additional hour of parent communication is associated with a +0.031 SD increase in self-efficacy (p < .001) and a +0.062 SD increase in parent-related stress (p < .001). PD participation in parent-collaboration topics shows positive main effects for self-efficacy and stress, but the key moderation result is that PD significantly weakens the communication–stress link (PD×Time = -0.040 SD, p < .001) while not significantly moderating communication–self-efficacy. The results are correlational (cross-sectional TALIS) and rely on self-reported outcomes, so causal claims cannot be made.
